\chapter{The Tense That Was Missing}
\label{ch:ar-the-tense-that-was-missing}
\hlchaptermodality{37}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can put a verb in the present tense for myself with the \ar{أ}- prefix, and I can say \ar{لا} \ar{أفهم} -- 'I do not understand' -- which is the sentence a beginner needs most and which this book was one form away from for six chapters.}

Eleven verbs taught as third-person past forms become first-person present forms, and each of them is then denied -- so a reading list turns into a speaking stock on one prefix.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[aktub]{\ar{أكتب} (aktub) — the tense that was missing}

\label{lesson:AR-C37-present}



\begin{quote}
Eleven verbs in this book and every one of them is a \textbf{past} tense, third person, masculine: \emph{kataba}, \textquotedblleft{}he wrote.\textquotedblright{} Nothing here has ever happened now, and nothing has ever happened to \textbf{you}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: the \ar{أ}- in front}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{كتب}} — \emph{kataba} — \textbf{he wrote} · \textbf{\ar{أكتب}} — \emph{aktub} — \textbf{I write}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{سأل}} — \emph{saʾala} — \textbf{he asked} · \textbf{\ar{أسأل}} — \emph{asʾal} — \textbf{I ask}
\end{quote}

The past tense marks who is speaking at the \textbf{end} of the word. The present marks it at the \textbf{front}, with a prefix, and \textbf{\ar{أ}} is the prefix for \emph{I}. Nothing is added at the back at all.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the front of the word, not the back}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{root} & \textbf{past, he} & \textbf{present, I} \\
\midrule
\ar{ك}-\ar{ت}-\ar{ب} & \textbf{\ar{كتب}} & \textbf{\ar{أكتب}} \\
\ar{س}-\ar{أ}-\ar{ل} & \textbf{\ar{سأل}} & \textbf{\ar{أسأل}} \\
\ar{ح}-\ar{ب}-\ar{ب} & \textbf{\ar{أحبّ}} & \textbf{\ar{أحبّ}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The third row is a warning as much as an example: \textbf{\ar{أحبّ}} is \emph{he loved} and \emph{I love} on the page, and only the vowels tell them apart — \emph{aḥabba} against \emph{uḥibb}. Arabic does not usually write those vowels. Context does the work, and this is where a reader starts needing it.

That \textbf{\ar{أ}} is old. Hebrew and Aramaic mark their first person the same way, at the front, with the same letter. It is older than either language.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \emph{kataba} … \emph{aktub}
  \item the second pair — \emph{saʾala} … \emph{asʾal}
  \item \emph{uḥibb} — I love
  \item the one this book most needs, in romanization — \emph{afham}, I understand
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the past tense mark the person, and where does the present? (\textbf{Past at the end; present at the front}.) Which letter is the prefix for \emph{I}? (\textbf{\ar{أ}}.) And why can \textbf{\ar{أحبّ}} be read two ways? (\textbf{The vowels that separate them are not written}.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lā afham]{\ar{لا} \ar{أفهم} (lā afham) — I do not understand}

\label{lesson:AR-C37-la-afham}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{لا}} has been in this book since chapter five, named there as the word that negates a present-tense verb. The book had no present-tense verb until the lesson before this one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} the item before this — the prefix that means \emph{I}, on \emph{aktub}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ar{لا} \ar{أفهم}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ar{لا} \ar{أفهم}} — \emph{lā afham} — \textbf{I do not understand.}
\end{quote}

Two words, and both halves were already in the book: \textbf{\ar{لا}} from chapter five, and \textbf{\ar{فهم}} — \emph{fahima}, \textquotedblleft{}he understood\textquotedblright{} — from chapter thirty-one. All that was missing was the prefix the last lesson taught.

\textbf{\ar{لا}} goes in \textbf{front} of the verb, which is where the chapter-five lesson said it goes, and the verb keeps its own shape.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the same operation on every verb you own}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{said} & \textbf{means} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ar{أكتب}} & I write \\
\textbf{\ar{لا} \ar{أكتب}} & I do not write \\
\textbf{\ar{لا} \ar{أسأل}} & I do not ask \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Nothing moves and nothing is added at the end. This is the operation a beginner uses more than any other, and this book could not perform it on any verb until this chapter.

One note on the page rather than the language: \textbf{\ar{فاء}}, the letter in the middle of \textbf{\ar{أفهم}}, has no lesson in this track's script ladder yet, so the sentence is printed whole here, in the lesson that owns it, and named in romanization wherever else it appears.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lā afham}
  \item the affirmative it denies — \emph{afham}
  \item \emph{lā aktub} … \emph{lā asʾal}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does \textbf{\ar{لا}} stand in relation to the verb? (\textbf{In front of it}.) Which two chapters supplied the halves of this sentence? (\textbf{Five}, for \textbf{\ar{لا}}, and \textbf{thirty-one}, for \textbf{\ar{فهم}}.) And what did the sentence need that neither of them had? (\textbf{The present tense}, from the lesson before this one.)

Source: \href{https://www.unicode.org/charts/PDF/U0600.pdf}{Unicode Arabic chart}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aktub · lā afham]{Now, and not}

\label{lesson:AR-R37-now-and-not}



\begin{quote}
Two items landed in this chapter and one of them was a whole tense. Name the prefix, and name the sentence it unlocked.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} three verbs in the past, as the book taught them — \emph{kataba, saʾala, fahima}
  \item \emph{Say it:} the same three in the present, for yourself — \emph{aktub, asʾal, afham}
  \item \emph{Say it:} each of them denied — \emph{lā aktub, lā asʾal, lā afham}
  \item \emph{Recall:} the very first verb this book taught, nine chapters back — \emph{dhahaba}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which end of the verb carries the person in the present tense? (\textbf{The front}.) Where does \textbf{\ar{لا}} go? (\textbf{In front of the whole verb}.) And how many new words did \emph{lā afham} need? (\textbf{None} — both halves were already taught, and only the tense was missing.)
\end{tcolorbox}
